title: Budget Bazaar: The Smart Spender Challenge
description: You just received 10,000 coins as pocket money for the whole school year! Can you manage your spending across school supplies, fun with friends, savings, and surprise emergencies over 10 months? Every choice matters — spend wisely and become a money master!

phases.name: tutorial
phases.description: Learn the basics of budgeting — needs vs. wants, first spending decisions, and handling surprises.

phases.name: core
phases.description: Apply your knowledge — resist sale temptations, review your finances, handle social pressure, and balance your budget.

phases.name: mastery
phases.description: Prove your money skills — earn income, give back, plan long-term, and reflect on your financial journey.

checkpoints.title: Budget Basics Check
checkpoints.description: Let us see what you have learned about budgeting so far! Answer these questions to unlock the next set of months.
checkpoints.review_summary: In the first five months, you learned to tell the difference between needs and wants, handled emergencies, made social spending choices, and explored whether to invest in learning or fun. These are the building blocks of smart money management.

questions.question: You have 500 coins left and need to buy school notebooks (200 coins) and a trendy phone case (300 coins). Your old phone case still works fine. What should you buy?

choices.label: Buy both — you need them equally
choices.explanation: The phone case is a want, not a need. Your old case still works! Notebooks are the real need here because you cannot do schoolwork without them.

choices.label: Buy only the notebooks — those are the real need
choices.explanation: Correct! Notebooks are a need for school, while a phone case when your old one works is a want. Smart budgeters always cover needs before wants.

choices.label: Buy neither and save all the money
choices.explanation: Saving is important, but not buying essential school supplies hurts your learning. You need to spend on true needs even when saving.

choices.label: Money you save to buy something expensive you really want
choices.explanation: That would be goal-based saving, not an emergency fund. An emergency fund is specifically for unexpected problems, not planned purchases.

choices.label: Money set aside for unexpected expenses like a broken phone or ruined project
choices.explanation: Exactly right! An emergency fund is your financial safety net. When something breaks or goes wrong unexpectedly, this money protects you from stress.

choices.label: The coins left over in your wallet at the end of each month
choices.explanation: Leftover money is not an emergency fund unless you deliberately move it into one. An emergency fund is money you set aside on purpose for surprises.

questions.question: A store has a 50% off sale on a cool jacket that normally costs 1,000 coins. You do not really need a new jacket. Is this a good deal?

choices.label: Yes! You save 500 coins by buying it on sale
choices.explanation: You are not saving 500 coins — you are spending 500 coins on something you do not need. A discount on something unnecessary is still wasted money.

choices.label: No — spending 500 coins on something you do not need is not saving money
choices.explanation: Correct! A sale is only a good deal if you actually need the item. Saving money on something you do not need is still spending money you did not have to.

choices.label: It depends on whether your friends are buying one too
choices.explanation: What your friends buy should not decide how you spend your money. That is peer pressure! Your budget should be based on your needs, not what others are doing.

questions.question: Your friend invites you to an expensive activity but you cannot afford it. What is the best thing to do?

choices.label: Go anyway and worry about money later
choices.explanation: Ignoring your budget to have fun now leads to bigger problems later. You might not have money when you really need it.

choices.label: Say no without explaining and hope they do not ask again
choices.explanation: It is okay to say no, but hiding the reason can hurt your friendship. Being open about your situation builds trust.

choices.label: Be honest that it is too expensive and suggest a cheaper or free alternative
choices.explanation: Great choice! Being honest about money builds real friendships. Suggesting an alternative shows you still want to spend time together without breaking your budget.

checkpoints.title: Smart Spender Final Quiz
checkpoints.description: You are nearly at the end of the school year! Let us test your advanced money skills before the final months.
checkpoints.review_summary: In the second half of the year, you explored earning money, giving to charity, handling social pressure with creativity, and planning for the future. You learned that money is a tool for living a meaningful life — it is about balance, not just saving every coin.

questions.question: You earned 300 coins from dog walking this month. A financial planner would suggest splitting your money into categories. Which split makes the most sense?

choices.label: Spend all 300 on fun — you earned it!
choices.explanation: You did earn it, but spending everything leaves nothing for needs, savings, or emergencies. Earning money teaches discipline, not just spending power.

choices.label: Save all 300 and do not spend any of it
choices.explanation: Saving everything sounds smart, but you need balance. If you never enjoy your money, you might lose motivation to keep earning and saving.

choices.label: Split it: 40% needs, 30% savings, 20% fun, 10% emergency fund
choices.explanation: This is the balanced approach! The 40-30-20-10 rule helps you cover your needs, build savings, enjoy life, and stay prepared for surprises. Financial planners recommend exactly this kind of split.

questions.question: Why is it better to earn money through your own work rather than just receiving pocket money?

choices.label: Because you get more money that way
choices.explanation: You might actually earn less than your pocket money! The real benefit is not the amount — it is how earning changes the way you think about spending.

choices.label: Because when you work for money, you understand its value and spend more carefully
choices.explanation: Exactly! When you know how hard it is to earn 100 coins, you think twice before spending them on something silly. Earning builds financial appreciation and discipline.

choices.label: Because your parents will stop giving you pocket money
choices.explanation: Earning money is not about replacing pocket money. It is about developing independence and understanding the real value of money through your own effort.

questions.question: Your class is collecting money for charity. You want to help but your budget is tight. What is the smartest approach?

choices.label: Give as much as the richest kid in class so nobody thinks you are cheap
choices.explanation: Giving more than you can afford to impress others is not generosity — it is peer pressure. Smart giving means giving what you can without hurting your own finances.

choices.label: Calculate a small percentage of your money to give, or volunteer your time instead
choices.explanation: Perfect! Planned giving (like donating 5% of your money) or volunteering time are both generous and sustainable. You help others without hurting yourself financially.

choices.label: Give nothing — you need all your money for yourself
choices.explanation: While protecting your budget is important, finding some way to help — even through time or small amounts — builds empathy and community. Generosity does not have to be expensive.

how_to_play: You are a Grade 6 student managing 10,000 coins of pocket money for the school year.
Each round is one month — you will face spending decisions about needs, wants, and savings.
Watch your dashboard! Your wallet, savings, happiness, and school supplies are all connected.
Random events like birthday parties or broken phones will test your planning skills.
NPCs (your parent, best friend, and teacher) will react to your choices and give advice.
Try to end the year with good savings, strong grades, and happy friendships!
learning_objectives: Understand the difference between needs and wants
Practice budgeting and planning spending over time
Learn the value of saving money and building an emergency fund
Develop strategic thinking about resource allocation
Build empathy through choices about sharing and helping others
Understand how financial decisions affect other areas of life
cultural_context: Global student life, personal finance, pocket money management

subsystems.label: Financial Health
subsystems.health_formula: min(100, max(0, min(100, savings / 100) * 0.4 + min(100, emergency_fund / 30) * 0.3 + financial_knowledge * 0.3))

tick_rules.label: Knowledge Grows

tick_rules.label: Savings Interest

tick_rules.label: Lonely Blues

interactions.label: Good Grades Confidence
interactions.description: Having the right supplies helps you do well in school, which makes you feel great!

interactions.label: Money Worries
interactions.description: Running low on money causes stress, which is not great for your health.

interactions.label: Smart Spending Habits
interactions.description: When you understand money better, you spend more wisely on school supplies too.

rounds.situation: It is the start of a brand-new school year! You have 10,000 coins of pocket money for the whole year. Your first challenge: buying school supplies. The store has everything from basic notebooks to fancy colored pens and a cool science kit. What do you buy?
rounds.goal: Set up for the school year by choosing what supplies to buy.
rounds.coaching_moment: Needs vs. Wants: School supplies are a need, but not every supply is equally necessary. Budgeting starts with telling the difference between what you need and what you want.
rounds.reflection_prompt: How do you decide what is a 'need' and what is a 'want' when shopping?
rounds.ai_image_prompt: Cartoon style, excited 11-year-old student in a colorful stationery store, shelves full of notebooks pens rulers, back-to-school vibes, bright cheerful

choices.label: A. Buy Everything on the List
choices.description: Get all the supplies your teacher recommended plus some extra cool stuff like a geometry set and colored markers. Costs 2,500 coins.

skill_explanation.risk_tolerance: Spending 25% of your yearly budget in one go is a bold financial gamble.
skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Buying everything upfront means planning to avoid future supply runs.

choices.feedback: You are fully stocked! But spending a quarter of your yearly budget in Month 1 is a big move. Will you have enough later?

choices.label: B. Just the Basics
choices.description: Buy only what you absolutely need — notebooks, pens, and a ruler. Costs 800 coins. You can always buy more later.

skill_explanation.delayed_gratification: Skipping the cool extras now keeps more coins available for later months.
skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Buying only essentials preserves your budget for unexpected needs ahead.

choices.feedback: Smart and careful! You saved money by buying only essentials. You can always get more supplies if you need them later.

choices.label: C. Buy Second-Hand Supplies
choices.description: An older student is selling last year's supplies at half price. They are used but perfectly fine. Costs 500 coins.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Finding a creative second-hand option shows you can adjust to save money.
skill_explanation.ethical_reasoning: Choosing reuse over new supports sustainability even if peers judge you.

choices.feedback: Recycling and saving money — double win! Some classmates might not understand, but reusing is smart and good for the planet.

choices.label: D. Save First, Buy Later
choices.description: Put 1,000 coins straight into savings before buying anything. Then buy basic supplies for 800 coins.

skill_explanation.delayed_gratification: Putting 1,000 coins into savings before shopping means future you wins.
skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: The 'pay yourself first' approach locks in savings before temptation hits.

choices.feedback: 'Pay yourself first' is a golden rule of money management! By saving before spending, you guarantee your future self has money.

rounds.situation: Your best friend Alex wants to go to the movies this weekend. Tickets cost 300 coins each, plus snacks. Another group of friends is going to an arcade — that is 500 coins. A third friend suggests a free picnic in the park instead. Everyone is watching to see what you choose.
rounds.goal: Balance social life with your budget.
rounds.coaching_moment: Peer Pressure & Spending: Friends can influence how we spend money. Real friends understand when you say 'I cannot afford that right now.' Spending to impress people is a trap.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Is it okay to say no to friends when something costs too much? How would you handle it?
rounds.ai_image_prompt: Cartoon style, group of diverse 11-year-old friends outside a movie theater and arcade, one student thinking with coins floating above their head, fun colorful scene

choices.label: A. Go to the Arcade
choices.description: The arcade is the most fun — everyone wants to go! Costs 500 coins.

skill_explanation.risk_tolerance: Dropping 500 coins on one afternoon is a high-stakes spend for fun.
skill_explanation.empathy: You chose the group activity so nobody feels left out of the plan.

choices.feedback: Maximum fun! Your social reputation soars. But 500 coins for one afternoon is a lot. Was it worth it?

choices.label: B. Movies with Alex
choices.description: A nice movie with your best friend. Costs 300 coins with snacks.

skill_explanation.adaptability: You found a middle-ground option that balances budget and social life.
skill_explanation.empathy: Prioritizing quality time with Alex shows you value your closest friendship.

choices.feedback: A balanced choice! Quality time with your best friend without breaking the bank. Smart social spending.

choices.label: C. Free Picnic in the Park
choices.description: Bring food from home and hang out in the park. Costs almost nothing!

skill_explanation.delayed_gratification: Choosing the free option now means more coins for bigger moments later.
skill_explanation.ethical_reasoning: Picking a zero-cost hangout respects your budget limits without pretending.

choices.feedback: The best things in life are free! Fresh air, good company, and you barely spent anything. Not everyone appreciates this yet, but it is wise.

choices.label: D. Suggest Everyone Splits Costs
choices.description: Propose that the group goes to the arcade but splits the cost — each person pays 250 coins. You organize it.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Proposing a cost-split gets the best experience for half the price.
skill_explanation.empathy: You made the fun affordable so every friend can join without stress.

choices.feedback: Leadership move! You found a way for everyone to have fun while spending less. That is real problem-solving.

rounds.situation: Bad news — you accidentally spilled water on your school project and your art folder is ruined! You need to redo the project, which requires new art supplies costing 700 coins. The project is due in 3 days. Also, your shoes are wearing out and new ones cost 1,200 coins.
rounds.goal: Handle an unexpected expense without panicking.
rounds.coaching_moment: Emergency Planning: Unexpected expenses happen to everyone. Having an emergency fund or knowing how to prioritize urgent vs. important expenses is a life skill.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why is it important to have money set aside for emergencies? What happens if you do not?
rounds.ai_image_prompt: Cartoon style, worried student looking at a ruined school project with water spilled on it, art supplies scattered, torn shoes nearby, dramatic but kid-friendly

choices.label: A. Fix Both — Project and Shoes
choices.description: Buy new art supplies (700 coins) AND new shoes (1,200 coins). Total: 1,900 coins.

skill_explanation.risk_tolerance: Spending 1,900 coins at once to fix everything is a big financial risk.
skill_explanation.adaptability: You responded quickly to two emergencies at the same time without hesitating.

choices.feedback: You solved both problems! But that was nearly 2,000 coins in one go. Check your wallet — can you still make it through the year?

choices.label: B. Fix the Project, Tape the Shoes
choices.description: Buy art supplies for the project (700 coins). Use tape and glue to fix the shoes for now.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Prioritizing the urgent deadline over worn shoes shows smart triage.
skill_explanation.resilience: Taping your shoes instead of replacing them means toughing it out to save.

choices.feedback: Good prioritizing! The project has a deadline, shoes can wait. Fixing things instead of replacing them saves money.

choices.label: C. Tap Your Emergency Fund
choices.description: If you have money in your emergency fund, use it! This is exactly what it is for.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Using the emergency fund for its exact purpose shows disciplined planning.
skill_explanation.delayed_gratification: Your earlier sacrifice of saving paid off now when you truly needed it.

choices.feedback: This is exactly what an emergency fund is for! You planned ahead and now you do not have to stress. Smart move!

choices.label: D. Ask for Help
choices.description: Ask your parent if they can help with the shoes, and borrow art supplies from a classmate for the project.

skill_explanation.resilience: Swallowing your pride to ask for help when broke takes real courage.
skill_explanation.empathy: Borrowing from a classmate means trusting others and accepting vulnerability.

choices.feedback: Asking for help is not weakness — it is wisdom! But relying on others too much can be uncomfortable. Building your own safety net is the long-term goal.

rounds.situation: Your wallet is nearly empty and there are still months left in the school year! Your parent noticed and wants to talk. You feel stressed because your friends keep inviting you to things you cannot afford. What do you do?
rounds.goal: Find a way to stretch your remaining money and recover from overspending.
rounds.coaching_moment: Financial Recovery: Running out of money feels scary, but it is not the end. The important thing is to recognize the problem, make a plan, and stick to it. Every adult has had to recover from overspending at some point.
rounds.reflection_prompt: When you realize you have spent too much, what is the first thing you should do?
rounds.ai_image_prompt: Cartoon style, worried student with an almost empty piggy bank, parent sitting beside them at kitchen table, calculator and coins, supportive atmosphere, kid-friendly

choices.label: A. Make a Strict Budget Plan
choices.description: Sit down with your parent and create a spending plan for every remaining month. No fun purchases until you are stable.
choices.feedback: Tough but smart! A budget plan is the foundation of financial recovery. It is not fun now, but future-you will be grateful.

skill_explanation.resilience: Pushing through difficulty builds mental strength.
skill_explanation.delayed_gratification: Investing effort now for later payoff builds discipline.

choices.label: B. Find Ways to Earn Extra
choices.description: Offer to do extra chores, help a neighbor, or sell some old toys and books you do not use anymore.
choices.feedback: Entrepreneurial spirit! Earning money teaches you the value of every coin. When you work for money, you think twice before spending it.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Adjusting your approach when conditions change shows flexibility.
skill_explanation.resilience: Choosing to persist when things get hard develops resilience.

choices.label: C. Ask for an Advance on Next Month
choices.description: Ask your parent for next month's pocket money early. You promise to be more careful.
choices.feedback: Borrowing from the future is tempting but dangerous. You got money now, but next month will be tighter. Be careful with this habit!

skill_explanation.risk_tolerance: Evaluating risk vs. reward is a key life skill.
skill_explanation.empathy: Valuing others' experiences alongside your own shows empathetic thinking.

choices.label: D. Budget Plan + Earn a Little Extra
choices.description: Make a budget plan AND do a few odd jobs to earn some extra coins. It is more work, but covers both sides.
choices.feedback: The best of both worlds! Planning your spending AND increasing your income is how adults actually manage money. Great thinking!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.
skill_explanation.resilience: Learning from setbacks rather than giving up shows resilience.

rounds.situation: Your school is offering a special 4-week financial literacy workshop after school. It costs 400 coins but teaches you about saving, investing, and budgeting. At the same time, there is a really popular video game everyone is buying for 600 coins.
rounds.goal: Choose between investing in your knowledge or buying something fun.
rounds.coaching_moment: Investing in Yourself: The best investment you can ever make is in learning. Knowledge grows forever, but a video game gets boring eventually.
rounds.reflection_prompt: What is the difference between spending money and investing money? Can you invest in yourself?
rounds.ai_image_prompt: Cartoon style, split scene showing student in a classroom learning about money on one side and playing video games on the other, thought bubble with question mark, colorful

choices.label: A. Take the Financial Literacy Workshop
choices.description: Pay 400 coins for 4 weeks of money skills. You will learn about budgets, saving, and even how banks work!
choices.feedback: Incredible choice! This knowledge will save you thousands of coins over your lifetime. The workshop gives you tools that last forever.

skill_explanation.delayed_gratification: Resisting the quick fix in favor of lasting results shows maturity.
skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

choices.label: B. Buy the Video Game
choices.description: Everyone is talking about this game! It costs 600 coins. You will be the coolest kid in class for a few weeks.
choices.feedback: Fun now! Your friends are impressed. But trends change fast — next month there will be a new game. Was this the best use of 600 coins?

skill_explanation.risk_tolerance: Taking a calculated risk shows you can handle uncertainty.
skill_explanation.empathy: Considering how others feel shows emotional intelligence.

choices.label: C. Workshop + Save Up for the Game
choices.description: Take the workshop now (400 coins) and set a goal to save 600 coins for the game over the next 2 months.
choices.feedback: Goal-setting champion! You chose knowledge first AND made a plan for fun. This is how smart spenders think.

skill_explanation.delayed_gratification: Waiting for the right moment instead of rushing shows self-control.
skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

choices.label: D. Skip Both, Save the Money
choices.description: Put 500 coins into your savings instead. You can always learn about money from free online videos.
choices.feedback: Disciplined saving! But be careful not to say no to everything. Sometimes spending on learning or experiences is worth it.

skill_explanation.delayed_gratification: Prioritizing long-term gains over short-term comfort builds character.
skill_explanation.resilience: Staying focused under pressure builds your ability to bounce back.

rounds.situation: A massive holiday sale is happening! Everything is 50% off. You spot an amazing backpack (normally 1,000, now 500 coins), a cool watch (normally 800, now 400 coins), and new sneakers (normally 1,500, now 750 coins). Your old backpack still works fine but is not as cool.
rounds.goal: Resist temptation and make smart choices about sale shopping.
rounds.coaching_moment: Sale Traps: A 50% discount is only a good deal if you actually need the item. Saving money on something you do not need is still spending money you did not have to.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Just because something is on sale, does that mean you should buy it? How do you decide?
rounds.ai_image_prompt: Cartoon style, colorful store with huge SALE signs, excited student looking at shiny backpack watch and sneakers, price tags with crossed-out prices, tempting display

choices.label: A. Buy Everything — It Is 50% Off!
choices.description: Grab the backpack (500), watch (400), and sneakers (750). Total: 1,650 coins. These deals are too good to miss!
choices.feedback: Wow, you went all in! You look amazing, but you just spent a lot on things you did not really need. 'Saving money' by spending money is a common trap.

skill_explanation.risk_tolerance: Stepping outside your comfort zone builds risk assessment skills.
skill_explanation.empathy: Taking others' perspectives into account builds empathy.

choices.label: B. Just the Sneakers — You Actually Need Those
choices.description: Your current shoes are falling apart. The sneakers at 750 coins are a genuine need on sale.
choices.feedback: Smart shopper! You bought what you actually needed and saved over 50%. That is the right way to use a sale.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.
skill_explanation.delayed_gratification: Choosing a future benefit over an immediate reward shows patience.

choices.label: C. Walk Away — You Do Not Need Any of It
choices.description: Your stuff still works. You do not need new things just because they are on sale. Save your money!
choices.feedback: Iron willpower! Walking away from a sale is one of the hardest money skills. You just proved you control your spending, not the other way around.

skill_explanation.delayed_gratification: Investing effort now for later payoff builds discipline.
skill_explanation.resilience: Facing challenges head-on strengthens your resilience over time.

choices.label: D. Backpack + Put the Savings in Emergency Fund
choices.description: Buy the backpack (500 coins) since yours is getting worn. Put 500 coins from the money you did not spend into your emergency fund.
choices.feedback: Brilliant strategy! You treated yourself a little AND strengthened your safety net. This is balanced spending at its best.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.
skill_explanation.delayed_gratification: Resisting the quick fix in favor of lasting results shows maturity.

rounds.situation: Halfway through the school year! Time to check in. Your teacher asked everyone to write about what they have learned about money this year. As you think about it, you realize you have some important choices to make for the second half of the year.
rounds.goal: Reflect on your spending so far and set a strategy for the rest of the year.
rounds.coaching_moment: Financial Check-Ups: Just like a doctor's check-up, your money needs regular reviews. Looking at where your money went helps you make better choices going forward.
rounds.reflection_prompt: If you could go back to Month 1, what would you do differently with your money?
rounds.ai_image_prompt: Cartoon style, student at desk with notebook writing a midyear reflection, pie chart of spending on the wall, calendar showing 6 months passed, thoughtful expression, bright classroom

choices.label: A. Savings Sprint — Save Hard for 2 Months
choices.description: Commit to spending only on essentials for the next 2 months and put everything extra into savings.
choices.feedback: Aggressive saving! It will be a quiet couple of months, but your savings will thank you. Sometimes sacrifice now means freedom later.

skill_explanation.delayed_gratification: Waiting for the right moment instead of rushing shows self-control.
skill_explanation.resilience: Pushing through difficulty builds mental strength.

choices.label: B. Balanced Plan — A Little of Everything
choices.description: Split your remaining money: 40% needs, 30% savings, 20% fun, 10% emergency fund.
choices.feedback: The 40-30-20-10 rule! This is how financial planners actually recommend splitting your money. You are thinking like a pro.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.
skill_explanation.adaptability: Being open to new information and changing course builds adaptability.

choices.label: C. Invest in Academics — Stock Up on Supplies
choices.description: Spend 600 coins on all the supplies you need for second semester. Your grades need a boost.
choices.feedback: Investing in education is always smart. Good supplies lead to better work, better grades, and more confidence.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.
skill_explanation.delayed_gratification: Prioritizing long-term gains over short-term comfort builds character.

choices.label: D. Build the Emergency Fund
choices.description: Move 1,000 coins into your emergency fund. After the cracked phone and ruined project, you know surprises happen!
choices.feedback: Learning from experience! You had emergencies and now you are preparing for the next one. That is real financial maturity.

skill_explanation.delayed_gratification: Choosing a future benefit over an immediate reward shows patience.
skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

rounds.situation: Things have gotten tough socially. You have been saying no to everything to save money, and now some classmates are whispering that you are 'cheap' or 'boring.' Alex is hurt because you have not hung out in weeks. You overhear someone say they do not want you in their group project. This feels terrible.
rounds.goal: Find a way to rebuild friendships without destroying your budget.
rounds.coaching_moment: Money and Relationships: Friendships should not cost money, but being social sometimes does. The key is finding creative ways to connect that do not require spending a lot.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Can you be a good friend without spending a lot of money? What are some free ways to show you care?
rounds.ai_image_prompt: Cartoon style, sad student sitting alone at lunch table while other kids talk in groups, thought bubble showing coins vs friends, emotional but kid-friendly, school cafeteria

choices.label: A. Throw a Party to Win Everyone Back
choices.description: Host a pizza party for your class. Costs 800 coins, but it will make everyone like you again instantly.
choices.feedback: The party worked! Everyone loves you again... for now. But buying friendship is expensive and does not last. Real friendship is not about money.

skill_explanation.risk_tolerance: Being willing to try something uncertain develops risk tolerance.
skill_explanation.empathy: Understanding the impact on people around you shows care for others.

choices.label: B. Have an Honest Talk with Alex
choices.description: Tell Alex the truth — you have been saving money and it is hard to say no all the time. Ask to find free things to do together.
choices.feedback: Being honest about money is brave and builds real trust. Alex understands and suggests free activities. This is what true friendship looks like.

skill_explanation.empathy: Listening to different viewpoints strengthens your empathy skills.
skill_explanation.resilience: Choosing to persist when things get hard develops resilience.

choices.label: C. Organize Free Group Activities
choices.description: Start a board game club, organize park hangouts, or create a study group. Show that fun does not need to cost money.
choices.feedback: Leadership move! You created fun that is free for everyone. Classmates actually think this is cooler than spending money. You just changed the social game!

skill_explanation.adaptability: Pivoting your strategy when needed is a sign of adaptive thinking.
skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

choices.label: D. Small but Thoughtful Gestures
choices.description: Make handmade cards for friends, share your lunch, help with homework. Spend time, not money — costs just 100 coins for craft supplies.
choices.feedback: The most meaningful gifts are personal, not expensive. Your handmade cards mean more than any store-bought present. Kindness is free!

skill_explanation.empathy: Valuing others' experiences alongside your own shows empathetic thinking.
skill_explanation.ethical_reasoning: Choosing what's right over what's easy shows moral courage.

rounds.situation: You have an idea! What if you could earn some extra money? Your neighbor needs help walking their dog (50 coins/week). The school has a recycling drive that pays 30 coins per bag collected. And your parent says you can earn money by doing extra chores beyond your normal ones.
rounds.goal: Explore ways to earn money and understand the value of work.
rounds.coaching_moment: Earning vs. Receiving: When you earn money through your own effort, you value it much more. Understanding where money comes from is just as important as knowing how to spend it.
rounds.reflection_prompt: How does earning money yourself change the way you think about spending it?
rounds.ai_image_prompt: Cartoon style, energetic student walking a dog in the neighborhood while another kid collects recycling, coins appearing like rewards, sunny positive scene, entrepreneurial vibes

choices.label: A. Dog Walking Business
choices.description: Walk the neighbor's dog every day after school. You earn 200 coins this month but it takes time and energy.
choices.feedback: Your first business! You earned money AND got exercise. But the time spent means less study time. Balancing work and school is a real adult skill.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Responding to unexpected situations with creativity shows adaptability.
skill_explanation.resilience: Learning from setbacks rather than giving up shows resilience.

choices.label: B. Recycling Champion
choices.description: Collect recyclable materials from your neighborhood. You earn 150 coins and help the environment!
choices.feedback: Making money while saving the planet! Recycling teaches that value exists in things people throw away. Entrepreneurship can be green!

skill_explanation.ethical_reasoning: Considering fairness in your decision demonstrates ethical thinking.
skill_explanation.adaptability: Flexibility in your thinking helps you handle change effectively.

choices.label: C. Tutoring Younger Students
choices.description: Help Grade 4 students with their homework for 250 coins/month. You are good at math!
choices.feedback: Teaching is the highest form of learning! You earned money, helped others, and reinforced your own knowledge. Triple win!

requires.label: Requires School Supplies >= 40 (need to be a strong student to tutor)

skill_explanation.empathy: Considering how others feel shows emotional intelligence.
skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

choices.label: D. Cut Spending Instead of Earning
choices.description: Rather than working, find ways to spend less — bring lunch from home, borrow books from the library, walk instead of taking the bus.
choices.feedback: A coin saved is a coin earned! Cutting expenses is often easier than earning more. Both skills are important, but frugality is free.

skill_explanation.delayed_gratification: Investing effort now for later payoff builds discipline.
skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

rounds.situation: The school is running a charity drive for a local shelter. A classmate's family lost their home in a storm and needs help. Your class is also collecting for a gift for your retiring teacher. Everyone is looking at everyone else to see who gives what.
rounds.goal: Decide how and how much to give to others.
rounds.coaching_moment: Generosity and Budgeting: Giving to others feels wonderful and is important. But you also need to take care of yourself first. Smart givers plan their generosity like they plan their spending.
rounds.reflection_prompt: How do you decide how much to give when someone needs help? Is it okay to give less than others if that is what you can afford?
rounds.ai_image_prompt: Cartoon style, students organizing a charity drive at school, collection boxes, donation items, diverse kids helping together, warm community feeling, classroom decorated with giving theme posters

choices.label: A. Give Generously to All Three
choices.description: Donate 500 coins total — 200 to the shelter, 200 to your classmate, and 100 for the teacher gift.
choices.feedback: What a generous heart! Giving feels amazing. Just make sure you have enough left for your own needs too.

skill_explanation.empathy: Taking others' perspectives into account builds empathy.
skill_explanation.ethical_reasoning: Weighing the ethical implications shows principled reasoning.

choices.label: B. Budget Your Giving — 5% of Wallet
choices.description: Calculate 5% of your current wallet and split it between the three causes. It is fair and sustainable.
choices.feedback: Planned giving! Many adults use the 5-10% rule for charity. You are learning that generosity can be both heartfelt and calculated.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.
skill_explanation.ethical_reasoning: Standing by your values even under pressure builds integrity.

choices.label: C. Give Time, Not Money
choices.description: Volunteer at the shelter for a day, help your classmate's family move, and organize a thank-you letter for the teacher. Costs nothing.
choices.feedback: Time is the most precious gift! Volunteers are the backbone of every community. You gave something money cannot buy — your energy and care.

skill_explanation.empathy: Understanding the impact on people around you shows care for others.
skill_explanation.adaptability: Adjusting your approach when conditions change shows flexibility.

choices.label: D. Focus on the Classmate in Need
choices.description: Give 300 coins directly to your classmate's family. They need it most right now.
choices.feedback: Prioritizing the most urgent need shows real empathy. Your classmate will always remember your kindness. Direct help makes the biggest immediate impact.

skill_explanation.empathy: Listening to different viewpoints strengthens your empathy skills.
skill_explanation.ethical_reasoning: Thinking about what's fair for everyone involved shows ethical awareness.

rounds.situation: Only 2 months left! You start thinking about the future. Next year, school fees might go up. Your family is talking about a summer trip. You also want to buy something special for yourself — a reward for getting through the year. How do you plan?
rounds.goal: Think long-term and set financial goals beyond this school year.
rounds.coaching_moment: Long-Term Thinking: Money is not just about today. The best financial thinkers plan weeks, months, and even years ahead. Setting goals gives your money a purpose.
rounds.reflection_prompt: What is one financial goal you could set for next year? How would you start working toward it now?
rounds.ai_image_prompt: Cartoon style, student drawing a vision board with goals, piggy bank growing bigger, calendar showing future months, dreaming about summer trip and new school year, optimistic bright scene

choices.label: A. Start a Summer Trip Fund
choices.description: Put 500 coins aside specifically for the family summer trip. Label it 'Summer Fun!'
choices.feedback: Goal-based saving! When you save for something specific, you are more motivated. A summer trip fund gives your savings a purpose.

skill_explanation.delayed_gratification: Resisting the quick fix in favor of lasting results shows maturity.
skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

choices.label: B. Save for Next Year's Supplies
choices.description: Set aside 600 coins for next year. You will not have to worry about Month 1 supplies next time!
choices.feedback: Planning a whole year ahead? That is next-level thinking! Future-you is going to be so thankful for this decision.

skill_explanation.delayed_gratification: Waiting for the right moment instead of rushing shows self-control.
skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

choices.label: C. Reward Yourself — You Earned It!
choices.description: Buy yourself something special for making it this far. A book, a game, or a treat — up to 400 coins.
choices.feedback: You deserve it! Rewarding yourself for good financial behavior is actually smart — it keeps you motivated. Just do not go overboard!

skill_explanation.adaptability: Being open to new information and changing course builds adaptability.
skill_explanation.resilience: Staying focused under pressure builds your ability to bounce back.

choices.label: D. The Big Move — Invest Everything Extra
choices.description: Put ALL spare money into savings and emergency fund. No fun spending this month. Total financial discipline.
choices.feedback: Maximum financial power! But remember — money is a tool for living, not the goal of living. Balance is important.

skill_explanation.delayed_gratification: Prioritizing long-term gains over short-term comfort builds character.
skill_explanation.resilience: Facing challenges head-on strengthens your resilience over time.

rounds.situation: The school year is ending! Time for the final accounting. You look at your savings, your wallet, your emergency fund, and all the experiences you had. Your teacher asks everyone to share one money lesson they learned. Your parent asks what you are most proud of financially.
rounds.goal: Make one final choice that reflects everything you have learned about money.
rounds.coaching_moment: Legacy & Values: In the end, money is just a tool. What matters is what you did with it — the supplies that helped you learn, the fun with friends, the savings for the future, and the help you gave others. Your relationship with money reflects your values.
rounds.reflection_prompt: If you could give one piece of money advice to a younger student, what would it be?
rounds.ai_image_prompt: Cartoon style, proud student at end of school year, trophy and report card in hand, piggy bank with savings, friends around, parent smiling, bright graduation-like celebration, achievement unlocked vibes

choices.label: A. Teach a Money Class for Younger Students
choices.description: Use what you learned to teach Grade 4 and 5 students about budgeting. It costs nothing and gives everything.
choices.feedback: Teaching others is the ultimate proof that you truly learned something. You are paying it forward — the most valuable investment of all.

skill_explanation.empathy: Valuing others' experiences alongside your own shows empathetic thinking.
skill_explanation.ethical_reasoning: Choosing what's right over what's easy shows moral courage.

choices.label: B. Set a 5,000-Coin Savings Target for Next Year
choices.description: Create a plan to save 5,000 coins next year. Write it down, break it into monthly goals, and commit.
choices.feedback: A written goal is 10 times more likely to be achieved than a vague wish. You just turned a dream into a plan. Financial maturity unlocked!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.
skill_explanation.delayed_gratification: Choosing a future benefit over an immediate reward shows patience.

choices.label: C. Celebrate with Friends — End-of-Year Party!
choices.description: Throw a small end-of-year celebration with your friends. Share food, play games, and celebrate together. Costs 300 coins.
choices.feedback: Money is a tool for creating joy! Celebrating with people you care about is one of the best uses of money. You earned this party.

skill_explanation.empathy: Considering how others feel shows emotional intelligence.
skill_explanation.adaptability: Pivoting your strategy when needed is a sign of adaptive thinking.

choices.label: D. The Full Circle — Save, Share, and Celebrate
choices.description: Split your remaining energy three ways: save 200 coins, donate 100 coins to the school fund, and spend 100 coins on a small treat for yourself and Alex.
choices.feedback: Balance, generosity, and self-care — all in one move. You just demonstrated that money is a tool for living a complete, meaningful life. Congratulations!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.
skill_explanation.ethical_reasoning: Considering fairness in your decision demonstrates ethical thinking.

achievements.label: Balanced Life
achievements.condition: happiness >= 55 and health >= 55 and savings >= 2000 and school_supplies >= 50

glossary_terms.definition: A plan for how you will spend and save your money over a period of time. A budget helps you make sure you have enough for what you need.
Needs are things you must have (food, school supplies, shoes). Wants are things that are nice to have but not essential (video games, fancy backpack).
Money you set aside specifically for unexpected expenses, like a broken phone or a sudden school project cost. It is your financial safety net.
Money you do not spend right away, but keep for the future. Savings grow over time, especially when they earn interest.
Extra money a bank pays you for keeping your savings with them. It is like a reward for saving! Your money earns money.
When friends or classmates influence you to do something — like spending money — to fit in. It is important to make your own choices.
When you choose to spend money on one thing, you give up the chance to spend it on something else. Every choice has a trade-off.
The knowledge and skills to make smart decisions about money — budgeting, saving, spending wisely, and planning for the future.

endings.title: Financial Wizard!
endings.message: Incredible! You ended the school year with a strong savings account and deep financial knowledge. Your parent is amazed, your teacher is proud, and you have set yourself up for an amazing next year. You proved that understanding money is a superpower. Other students come to you for advice — you are the class money expert!

endings.title: Social Butterfly!
endings.message: You are the most popular kid in class! Your friendships are strong, you are always invited to everything, and people love being around you. You learned that the best social experiences do not always cost the most money. Your happiness and kindness made you a magnet for great friendships.

endings.title: Scholar's Path!
endings.message: Your academic performance soared this year! With the right supplies and growing financial knowledge, you became one of the top students. Your teacher nominated you for a scholarship. You proved that investing in your education is the smartest financial decision a student can make.

endings.title: Emergency Ready Champion!
endings.message: You built an amazing emergency fund this year! While other students panicked when surprises came up, you were calm and prepared. Your parent calls you 'the planner' and your friends are impressed by how you handle unexpected situations. You learned the most important money lesson: always be prepared.

endings.title: Balanced Student
endings.message: You made it through the school year! It was not always perfect, but you learned valuable lessons about managing money. You had fun with friends, kept up with school, and started understanding how to budget. The most important thing is what you learned along the way — and that knowledge will serve you for the rest of your life.

reflection_prompt: Which lever, if you'd moved it earlier, would have changed your outcome the most?
